summary: Hebrew’s three most frequent prepositions are single letters written onto the next word: בְּ “in, at” (also “with” a tool), לְ “to, for” and מִ “from”. The others are separate words: עִם “with”, בְּלִי “without”, בִּשְׁבִיל “for”, עַל “about” (and “on”, lesson 12), אֵצֶל “at someone’s (place)”, and the formal אֶל “to”. בְּ and לְ swallow the article: בְּ + הַבַּיִת → בַּבַּיִת “at home, in the house”, לְ + הַשּׁוּק → לַשּׁוּק “to the market” — the ה disappears and its vowel moves to the prefix. מִ does not: מֵהַבַּיִת “from the house”. The prefixes also change their vowel: בִּ / לִ before a shva (בִּשְׂדֵה הַתְּעוּפָה), בַּ before a hataf patah (בַּחֲנוּת); מִ doubles the next letter (מִתֵּל אָבִיב) and becomes מֵ before ע, ח, א, ר and before the article (מֵחֵיפָה, מֵהַבַּיִת). The noun itself never changes for the preposition — Hebrew has no cases (see fn.case). With a pronoun, every preposition takes a personal ending: לִי “to me”, אִתִּי “with me”, אֶצְלִי “at my place”, בִּשְׁבִילִי “for me”. The person something is for and the tool something is done with are always phrases with a preposition (בִּשְׁבִיל אִמָּא, בְּעֵט): the verb never changes for them.

blocks.caption: With a pronoun the preposition takes an ending (עִם uses the stem אִתּ־).

blocks.title: בַּ = בְּ + הַ, לַ = לְ + הַ
blocks.text: בַּבַּיִת is “in the house / at home”, לַבַּיִת “to the house”. Never write *בְּהַבַּיִת or *לְהַבַּיִת. Before ה with qamats or segol the fused vowel follows the article: בָּעֲבוֹדָה, בָּעִיר, לָעֲבוֹדָה.

blocks.title: מִ does not swallow the article
blocks.text: מֵהַבַּיִת “from the house” — the ה stays. And מִ doubles the next letter: מִשְּׂמֹאל, מִתֵּל אָבִיב (only ע, ח, א, ר and ה refuse, and take מֵ).

blocks.title: עִם or בְּ?
blocks.text: עִם is “together with”: עִם חֲבֵרִים, קָפֶה עִם חָלָב. A tool or means takes בְּ: כּוֹתֵב בְּעֵט “writes with a pen”.

blocks.title: At school, at Grandma’s
blocks.text: A place takes בְּ: בְּבֵית הַסֵּפֶר, בַּבַּנְק. A person (and their home or office) takes אֵצֶל: אֵצֶל סָבְתָא, אֵצֶל הָרוֹפֵא — like German bei.

blocks.title: Compound nouns
blocks.text: In בֵּית סֵפֶר the article sits on the second word (בֵּית הַסֵּפֶר), so nothing fuses: בְּבֵית הַסֵּפֶר “at school”. Note the soft ב after the prefix: b’veit.

blocks.title: No case after a preposition
blocks.text: German needs a case after every preposition (mit dem Mann, in der Stadt, in die Stadt). Hebrew needs none: הָאִישׁ stays הָאִישׁ after any preposition — only the first letters of the word may change spelling (בַּ, לַ, a doubled letter after מִ).

items.def: the form of a word right after an attached preposition, where it differs from the plain form: the definite form without its ה after בַּ / לַ (הַשּׁוּק → בַּשּׁוּק), or the first letter doubled after מִ (שְׂמֹאל → מִשְּׂמֹאל).

blocks.title: Ask yourself
questions: Is it in / at a place (בְּ), towards (לְ), or out of (מִ)?
Is there an article? → בַּ / לַ swallow it; מֵהַ keeps it.
Is it a person’s place? → אֵצֶל.
Together with (עִם) or by means of (בְּ)?

askYourself: Where is it? → בְּ (in, at): בַּבַּיִת, בָּעֲבוֹדָה. At a person’s? → אֵצֶל.
Where to / to whom / for whom? → לְ: לַשּׁוּק, לְאִמָּא (formal אֶל); “for” a person or purpose → בִּשְׁבִיל.
From where / from whom? → מִ (מֵ before ע ח א ר ה): מִתֵּל אָבִיב, מֵהַבַּיִת.
Together with? → עִם. Without? → בְּלִי. About a topic? → עַל.
Does the noun have the article? → with בְּ / לְ the ה falls away (בַּ / לַ); with מִ it stays (מֵהַ).
Does the prefix stand before a shva or a hataf? → בִּ / לִ before a shva, בַּ before a hataf patah.
Is it a pronoun (me, you …)? → use the preposition with its ending: לִי, אִתִּי, אֶצְלִי, בִּשְׁבִילִי.
steps: Attach בְּ / לְ / מִ, or write the separate word.
Fuse the article with בְּ / לְ; keep it after מִ.

traps: A tool takes בְּ, not עִם: בְּעֵט “with a pen”.
For people use אֵצֶל, not בְּ: אֵצֶל הָרוֹפֵא “at the doctor’s”.
בְּלִי is one word — not בְּ + לִי.
Unvowelled, בבית can be בְּבַיִת “in a house” or בַּבַּיִת “at home”: only the vowel shows the article.
“With me” is אִתִּי (not *עִם אֲנִי); “for me” is בִּשְׁבִילִי; “to me” is לִי.

quiz.why: בְּ + הַ fuse into בַּ: the ה disappears.
מִ does not fuse with the article: מֵ + הַבַּיִת.

quiz.q: Greek “Είμαι στου παππού” (I’m at Grandpa’s) — which Hebrew word for “at”?
quiz.why: At a person’s place Hebrew uses אֵצֶל: אֲנִי אֵצֶל סַבָּא.
A tool takes בְּ; עִם is “together with”.
Prepositions take personal endings; עִם uses the stem אִתּ־: אִתִּי, אִתְּךָ, אִתָּהּ. לִי is “to me”.

seeAlso.note: Arabic has the same prefixes بِـ and لِـ and the word مِنْ “from” (Hebrew מִן / מִ), but keeps the article (بِالْبَيْتِ) and puts the noun in the genitive -i after every preposition.
German in / an / zu / von / mit … each govern a case (mit dem, für den); Hebrew nouns never change after a preposition.
Chinese uses coverbs before the verb — 在 (at), 从 (from), 跟 (with), 给 (for) — where Hebrew uses prefixes and prepositions.

notes.text: Greek σε is three Hebrew words: בְּ (in, at: στο σπίτι ~ בַּבַּיִת), לְ (to: στο σχολείο ~ לְבֵית הַסֵּפֶר) and אֵצֶל (at someone’s: στου παππού ~ אֵצֶל סַבָּא); με is עִם (with someone) or בְּ (with a tool). And no case follows.
Russian prepositions demand a case (в доме, в дом, из дома); Hebrew ones change nothing in the noun. у бабушки “at Grandma’s” is אֵצֶל סָבְתָא.
en covers “in” and “at” like בְּ, and a + el → al fuses just as לְ + הַ → לַ (לַשּׁוּק “al mercado”); con is עִם, but “with a tool” is בְּ.
בְּ “in, at”, לְ “to” and מִ “from” work much like the English words, but they are written onto the next word and swallow the article (בַּבַּיִת). “With a pen” is בְּעֵט, not עִם.
As à + le → au, בְּ and לְ fuse with the article (בַּבַּיִת, לַשּׁוּק); chez is אֵצֶל (אֵצֶל סָבְתָא “chez mamie”).
bei is אֵצֶל, mit is עִם (or בְּ for a tool), and im / zum fuse like בַּ / לַ; but no case follows a Hebrew preposition.
Hindi puts postpositions after the noun (घर में, घर से, घर को); Hebrew puts prepositions before it and writes three of them onto it: בַּבַּיִת, מֵהַבַּיִת, לַבַּיִת.
Persian prepositions also come first (در خانه، از خانه، به خانه ~ בַּבַּיִת, מֵהַבַּיִת, לַבַּיִת); Hebrew writes בְּ, לְ, מִ onto the word.
Marathi attaches its endings to the noun (घरात “in the house”, घरातून “from the house”); Hebrew attaches prepositions to the front: בַּבַּיִת, מֵהַבַּיִת.
Arabic بِـ and لِـ are one-letter prefixes too (بِالْقَلَمِ, لِلْبَيْتِ), and مِنْ is “from”; Hebrew בְּ, לְ, מִ match them — but the noun after them takes no genitive ending.
Turkish uses case suffixes for in / to / from (evde, eve, evden); Hebrew uses prefixes on the other side: בַּבַּיִת, לַבַּיִת, מֵהַבַּיִת.
Japanese particles follow the noun (家で, 家に, 家から); Hebrew prepositions come before it, and three of them are written onto it.
Korean particles follow the noun (집에, 집에서); Hebrew prepositions precede it: בַּבַּיִת, מֵהַבַּיִת.
Finnish uses case endings (talossa, taloon, talosta); Hebrew uses prefixes before an unchanged noun: בַּבַּיִת, לַבַּיִת, מֵהַבַּיִת.
Hungarian uses case suffixes (házban, házba, házból); Hebrew uses prefixes: בַּבַּיִת, לַבַּיִת, מֵהַבַּיִת.

Swahili can add “for” to the verb itself (kupikia “to cook for”); Hebrew keeps the verb and adds a preposition: מְבַשֵּׁל בִּשְׁבִיל אִמָּא. Places take the ending -ni (nyumbani “at home”) where Hebrew uses בְּ.
Luganda can add “for someone” to the verb with an applicative extension; Hebrew keeps the verb as it is and adds בִּשְׁבִיל or לְ.
Chinese puts 在 / 从 / 到 before the place and often a location word after it (在桌子上); Hebrew uses one prefix: בַּבַּיִת, מִתֵּל אָבִיב.
Vietnamese prepositions also come first (ở nhà, từ Hà Nội); Hebrew writes בְּ, לְ, מִ onto the noun: בַּבַּיִת, מִתֵּל אָבִיב.
Inuktitut uses case endings (iglumi “in the house”, iglumut “to the house”, iglumit “from the house”); Hebrew uses the prefixes בְּ, לְ, מִ: בַּבַּיִת, לַבַּיִת, מֵהַבַּיִת.
